text: Johann Sebastian Bach was born in Eisenach, Germany, in 1685.
Bach had 20 children with his two wives; about half survived childhood.
Bach worked as Thomaskantor in Leipzig from 1723 until his death in 1750.
As a young man, Bach walked about 250 miles to Lübeck to hear organist Dieterich Buxtehude.
Bach's six Brandenburg Concertos were dedicated to the Margrave of Brandenburg in 1721.
Mendelssohn's 1829 performance of the St Matthew Passion sparked a Bach revival.
Bach's Goldberg Variations has 30 variations framed by an aria.
The Well-Tempered Clavier has preludes and fugues in all 24 major and minor keys.
Four of Bach's sons became composers, including C.P.E. and J.C. Bach.
Bach's Toccata and Fugue in D minor appears in Disney's Fantasia (1940).
Bach's music was included on the Voyager Golden Record launched in 1977.
Bach spent about a month in jail in Weimar in 1717 for demanding to leave his job.
George Frideric Handel was born in Halle in 1685, the same year as Bach.
Handel wrote Messiah in about 24 days in 1741.
Messiah premiered in Dublin, not London, in April 1742.
Handel became a British subject in 1727.
Handel is buried in Westminster Abbey.
Handel's Water Music was first played on a barge on the Thames in 1717.
Music for the Royal Fireworks celebrated the 1748 Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle.
Handel wrote over 40 operas, mostly in Italian.
Handel went blind late in life but kept performing on the organ.
Handel's London house on Brook Street is now a museum; Jimi Hendrix later lived next door.
Handel's Zadok the Priest has been sung at every British coronation since 1727.
Antonio Vivaldi was a Catholic priest, nicknamed 'the Red Priest' for his red hair.
Vivaldi taught music at the Ospedale della Pietà, a Venetian orphanage for girls.
Vivaldi's Four Seasons were published in 1725 with sonnets describing each season.
Vivaldi wrote about 500 concertos, around 230 of them for violin.
Vivaldi died poor in Vienna in 1741.
Much of Vivaldi's music was rediscovered only in the 20th century.
Joseph Haydn wrote 104 numbered symphonies.
Haydn is often called the 'Father of the Symphony' and of the string quartet.
Haydn served the wealthy Esterházy family for nearly 30 years.
Haydn's 'Surprise' Symphony No. 94 has a sudden loud chord in its slow movement.
In the 'Farewell' Symphony, musicians leave one by one, hinting the prince should let them go home.
Haydn's tune for 'Gott erhalte Franz den Kaiser' is now Germany's national anthem melody.
Haydn made two highly successful trips to London in the 1790s.
Haydn briefly taught the young Beethoven in Vienna.
Haydn's oratorio The Creation was inspired by hearing Handel in London.
Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was born in Salzburg in 1756.
Mozart wrote his first symphony at about age 8.
Mozart toured Europe as a child prodigy with his sister Nannerl.
In Rome, the teenage Mozart wrote down Allegri's secret Miserere after hearing it.
Mozart wrote over 600 works in a life of only 35 years.
Mozart's works are numbered by the Köchel catalogue, hence 'K.' numbers.
Mozart's last three symphonies were written in about six weeks in 1788.
Mozart died in 1791, leaving his Requiem unfinished.
Mozart's pupil Franz Xaver Süssmayr completed the Requiem.
The Magic Flute premiered just over two months before Mozart's death.
Mozart's Symphony No. 41 is nicknamed 'Jupiter', a title not given by Mozart.
Mozart's Clarinet Concerto was written for his friend Anton Stadler.
Mozart's opera librettist Lorenzo Da Ponte later emigrated and taught Italian at Columbia.
Mozart was a Freemason; The Magic Flute contains Masonic symbolism.
Ludwig van Beethoven was born in Bonn in 1770.
Beethoven wrote nine symphonies.
Beethoven began losing his hearing in his late twenties.
At the Ninth Symphony premiere, Beethoven had to be turned to see the applause.
Beethoven's Heiligenstadt Testament (1802) is a letter about his despair over deafness.
Beethoven first dedicated his Third Symphony to Napoleon, then scratched it out.
The 'Moonlight' Sonata's nickname came from critic Ludwig Rellstab after Beethoven's death.
Beethoven wrote only one opera, Fidelio.
Beethoven's Ninth ends with Schiller's 'Ode to Joy'.
'Ode to Joy' is the anthem of the European Union.
Beethoven's 'Für Elise' was published about 40 years after his death.
Beethoven used conversation books so visitors could write to him.
An estimated 10,000 or more people attended Beethoven's funeral in Vienna in 1827.
Beethoven wrote 32 piano sonatas.
Beethoven's Sixth Symphony, the 'Pastoral', depicts country life and a storm.
Beethoven's Fifth opens with a famous four-note motif: short-short-short-long.
Beethoven wrote 16 string quartets.
Beethoven never married.
Beethoven's 'Immortal Beloved' letter was found after his death; her identity is still debated.
Franz Schubert wrote over 600 songs.
Schubert died at just 31 in 1828.
Schubert's friends held musical evenings called 'Schubertiades'.
Schubert's 'Unfinished' Symphony has only two complete movements.
The 'Unfinished' Symphony premiered in 1865, 37 years after Schubert died.
Schubert set Goethe's 'Erlkönig' to music at about age 18.
Schubert was a torchbearer at Beethoven's funeral.
Schubert was buried near Beethoven at his own request.
Schubert's 'Trout' Quintet uses a double bass instead of a second violin.
Schubert's 'Ave Maria' was originally a setting of Walter Scott's poem.
Felix Mendelssohn wrote his Octet at age 16.
Mendelssohn wrote the Midsummer Night's Dream overture at 17.
Mendelssohn's 'Wedding March' is from his Midsummer Night's Dream music.
Mendelssohn founded the Leipzig Conservatory in 1843.
Mendelssohn's Hebrides Overture was inspired by Fingal's Cave in Scotland.
Mendelssohn died in 1847, months after his sister Fanny.
Mendelssohn was a favorite composer of Queen Victoria.
Frédéric Chopin was born near Warsaw in 1810.
Almost all of Chopin's music features the piano.
Chopin's heart was returned to Warsaw and rests in the Holy Cross Church.
Chopin had a nearly decade-long relationship with writer George Sand.
Chopin gave only about 30 public concerts in his life.
Chopin wrote his first published polonaise at age 7.
Chopin died in Paris at 39, likely of tuberculosis.
Chopin's 'Minute Waltz' takes longer than a minute; 'minute' means small.
Chopin wrote 21 nocturnes.
Chopin's funeral march is from his Piano Sonata No. 2.
Franz Liszt was born in Raiding, then in Hungary, in 1811.
Liszt is credited with inventing the solo piano recital.
Fans' frenzy at Liszt's concerts was called 'Lisztomania' by poet Heinrich Heine.
Liszt took minor orders in the Catholic Church and was called 'Abbé Liszt'.
Liszt's daughter Cosima married Richard Wagner.
Liszt wrote 19 Hungarian Rhapsodies for piano.
Liszt coined the term 'symphonic poem'.
Liszt taught many pupils without charging fees.
Robert Schumann injured his hand, ending his hopes as a concert pianist.
Robert Schumann founded a music journal, the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik.
Clara Schumann was one of the greatest pianists of the 19th century.
Clara Wieck married Robert Schumann in 1840 after a court battle with her father.
Schumann wrote about 140 songs in 1840, his 'year of song'.
Clara Schumann appeared on the German 100-mark banknote.
Robert Schumann praised the young Brahms in print as a coming genius.
Johannes Brahms was born in Hamburg in 1833.
Brahms took over 20 years to finish his First Symphony.
Brahms's First Symphony was nicknamed 'Beethoven's Tenth'.
Brahms's famous 'Lullaby' is 'Wiegenlied', Op. 49 No. 4.
Brahms never married but remained devoted to Clara Schumann.
Brahms wrote four symphonies.
Brahms destroyed many works he considered unworthy.
Brahms's Academic Festival Overture thanked the University of Breslau for an honorary degree.
Brahms's German Requiem uses German Bible texts rather than the Latin Mass.
Brahms's Hungarian Dances were his biggest commercial success.
Richard Wagner wrote both the music and the words for his operas.
Wagner's Ring cycle has four operas and lasts about 15 hours.
Wagner built his own theater, the Bayreuth Festspielhaus.
The Bayreuth Festival, devoted to Wagner's works, still runs every summer.
The 'Bridal Chorus' ('Here Comes the Bride') is from Wagner's Lohengrin.
Wagner used 'leitmotifs', musical themes tied to characters or ideas.
Wagner's 'Ride of the Valkyries' is from Die Walküre.
Wagner fled Dresden after taking part in the 1849 uprising.
The 'Tristan chord' is one of the most discussed chords in music history.
The Bayreuth orchestra plays in a covered pit hidden from the audience.
Giuseppe Verdi wrote 28 operas.
Verdi was rejected by the Milan Conservatory as a young man.
The chorus 'Va, pensiero' from Nabucco became a symbol of Italian patriotism.
'Viva Verdi' doubled as code for 'Viva Vittorio Emanuele Re D'Italia'.
Verdi's Aida premiered in Cairo in 1871.
Verdi wrote Falstaff, a comedy, at nearly 80.
Verdi founded a retirement home for musicians in Milan, Casa di Riposo.
Verdi and his wife Giuseppina are buried at the Casa di Riposo.
Verdi served as a member of Italy's first parliament.
'La donna è mobile' is from Verdi's Rigoletto.
Giacomo Puccini came from five generations of church musicians in Lucca.
Puccini died before finishing Turandot.
At Turandot's premiere, Toscanini stopped where Puccini's music ended.
Franco Alfano completed Puccini's Turandot.
'Nessun dorma' is from Puccini's Turandot.
Madama Butterfly's failed premiere led Puccini to revise it.
Puccini loved fast cars and hunting, and survived a serious car crash in 1903.
La bohème inspired the Broadway musical Rent.
Pyotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky studied law before turning to music.
Tchaikovsky was among the first graduates of the St Petersburg Conservatory.
Nadezhda von Meck supported Tchaikovsky for 13 years; they agreed never to meet.
Tchaikovsky conducted at the opening of Carnegie Hall in 1891.
Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture calls for cannon fire.
The Nutcracker introduced many to the celesta, used for the Sugar Plum Fairy.
Tchaikovsky died nine days after conducting his Sixth Symphony's premiere.
Swan Lake was not a success at its 1877 premiere.
Tchaikovsky wrote three ballets: Swan Lake, Sleeping Beauty and The Nutcracker.
Pianist Nikolai Rubinstein first called Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1 unplayable.
Tchaikovsky's Piano Concerto No. 1 premiered in Boston in 1875.
Antonín Dvořák was the son of a butcher and innkeeper in Bohemia.
Dvořák directed the National Conservatory in New York from 1892 to 1895.
Dvořák spent the summer of 1893 in Spillville, Iowa.
Dvořák's 'New World' Symphony was written in America.
Astronaut Neil Armstrong took a recording of the New World Symphony on Apollo 11.
Dvořák was a passionate trainspotter.
Brahms helped Dvořák find a publisher.
Bedřich Smetana's 'Vltava' (The Moldau) depicts a river flowing through Bohemia.
Smetana wrote much of Má vlast after becoming completely deaf.
Edvard Grieg's Piano Concerto in A minor is his only completed concerto.
'In the Hall of the Mountain King' is from Grieg's Peer Gynt.
Grieg was only about five feet tall.
Grieg's home, Troldhaugen near Bergen, is now a museum.
Jean Sibelius's Finlandia became a symbol of Finnish independence.
Sibelius wrote almost nothing for his last 30 years of life.
Sibelius is believed to have destroyed his Eighth Symphony.
Sibelius appeared on the Finnish 100-markka banknote.
Gustav Mahler was famous in his lifetime mainly as a conductor.
Mahler directed the Vienna Court Opera from 1897 to 1907.
Mahler conducted the New York Philharmonic and the Met late in life.
Mahler's Eighth is called the 'Symphony of a Thousand'.
Mahler composed in small huts in the countryside during summers.
Mahler's wife Alma was also a composer.
Mahler famously said a symphony 'must be like the world; it must embrace everything.'
Anton Bruckner was an organist who revised his symphonies many times.
Bruckner dedicated his Ninth Symphony 'to the beloved God'.
Bruckner is buried beneath the organ at St Florian Abbey.
Johann Strauss II was called the 'Waltz King'.
'The Blue Danube' was written by Johann Strauss II in 1866.
The Vienna New Year's Concert is built around the Strauss family's music.
Richard Strauss's 'Also sprach Zarathustra' opens 2001: A Space Odyssey.
Richard Strauss's father was a leading horn player in Munich.
Claude Debussy's 'Clair de lune' is from his Suite bergamasque.
Debussy won the Prix de Rome in 1884.
Debussy was fascinated by Javanese gamelan music he heard in Paris in 1889.
Debussy's only completed opera is Pelléas et Mélisande.
Debussy wrote Children's Corner for his daughter, nicknamed Chouchou.
The cover of Debussy's La mer used Hokusai's 'Great Wave'.
Maurice Ravel's Boléro repeats one melody, growing louder for about 15 minutes.
Ravel called Boléro 'a piece for orchestra without music'.
Ravel orchestrated Mussorgsky's Pictures at an Exhibition in 1922.
Ravel wrote a piano concerto for the left hand for Paul Wittgenstein.
Paul Wittgenstein lost his right arm in World War I.
Ravel was refused the Prix de Rome several times, causing a scandal in 1905.
Ravel toured the United States in 1928 and met George Gershwin.
Camille Saint-Saëns wrote The Carnival of the Animals but banned its publication in his lifetime.
'The Swan' from Carnival of the Animals was the only movement Saint-Saëns allowed published.
Saint-Saëns wrote the first film score by a major composer, in 1908.
Saint-Saëns's Organ Symphony was dedicated to Liszt's memory.
Georges Bizet died at 36, three months after Carmen's premiere.
Carmen was considered shocking at its premiere.
'Habanera' and the 'Toreador Song' are from Bizet's Carmen.
Gioachino Rossini wrote The Barber of Seville in about three weeks.
Rossini largely stopped writing operas at 37, after William Tell.
Rossini was a famous gourmet; Tournedos Rossini is named after him.
Rossini was born on February 29, 1792.
The William Tell Overture became the theme of The Lone Ranger.
Hector Berlioz's Symphonie fantastique was inspired by actress Harriet Smithson.
Berlioz later married Harriet Smithson.
Berlioz wrote an influential treatise on orchestration.
Berlioz trained in medicine before switching to music.
Modest Mussorgsky wrote Pictures at an Exhibition after visiting a memorial show of Viktor Hartmann's art.
Mussorgsky was part of 'The Five', a group of Russian nationalist composers.
Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov served as a naval officer while composing.
'Flight of the Bumblebee' is from Rimsky-Korsakov's opera Tsar Saltan.
Rimsky-Korsakov taught the young Igor Stravinsky.
Alexander Borodin was a chemist as well as a composer.
The musical Kismet borrowed melodies from Borodin.
Sergei Rachmaninoff had very large hands that could span a 13th on the keyboard.
Rachmaninoff dedicated his Second Piano Concerto to his therapist, Dr Nikolai Dahl.
Rachmaninoff left Russia after the 1917 revolution and later settled in the US.
Rachmaninoff became a US citizen weeks before he died in 1943.
The failed premiere of his First Symphony sent Rachmaninoff into depression.
The premiere of Stravinsky's The Rite of Spring in 1913 caused an uproar in Paris.
Stravinsky wrote three major ballets for Diaghilev's Ballets Russes.
Stravinsky became a US citizen in 1945.
Stravinsky is buried in Venice, near Diaghilev.
Stravinsky wrote a circus polka for an elephant ballet with Ringling Brothers.
Sergei Prokofiev wrote Peter and the Wolf to introduce children to the orchestra.
Prokofiev died on the same day as Joseph Stalin in 1953.
Prokofiev was also a strong chess player.
Prokofiev wrote his first opera at age 9.
Dmitri Shostakovich's Seventh Symphony premiered in besieged Leningrad in 1942.
Shostakovich was a volunteer firefighter during the siege of Leningrad.
Shostakovich was a lifelong soccer fan and a qualified referee.
Shostakovich wrote 15 symphonies and 15 string quartets.
Edward Elgar's Enigma Variations portray his friends.
'Nimrod' from the Enigma Variations depicts Elgar's friend August Jaeger.
'Land of Hope and Glory' uses the tune of Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance March No. 1.
In the US, Elgar's Pomp and Circumstance is played at graduations.
Elgar was largely self-taught as a composer.
Gustav Holst's The Planets has seven movements; Earth is not included.
Pluto was discovered in 1930, after Holst wrote The Planets.
Holst's 'Jupiter' supplied the hymn tune 'I Vow to Thee, My Country'.
Ralph Vaughan Williams collected English folk songs in the countryside.
Vaughan Williams edited The English Hymnal.
Vaughan Williams served as an ambulance driver in World War I.
George Gershwin's Rhapsody in Blue opens with a famous clarinet glissando.
Rhapsody in Blue premiered at Aeolian Hall in New York in 1924.
Gershwin's Porgy and Bess premiered in 1935.
Gershwin died of a brain tumor at 38.
An American in Paris uses real taxi horns.
Aaron Copland's Appalachian Spring won the 1945 Pulitzer Prize for Music.
Appalachian Spring uses the Shaker song 'Simple Gifts'.
Copland's 'Hoe-Down' from Rodeo became famous in beef commercials.
Copland studied in Paris with Nadia Boulanger.
Copland wrote Fanfare for the Common Man in 1942.
Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings began as a movement of his String Quartet.
Barber's Adagio was played at the funerals of FDR and Princess Grace.
Barber wrote his first opera at age 10.
Leonard Bernstein became famous overnight in 1943 when he substituted for Bruno Walter.
Bernstein's Young People's Concerts were televised by CBS.
Bernstein was the first American-born music director of the New York Philharmonic.
Bernstein conducted Beethoven's Ninth in Berlin in 1989, singing 'Freiheit' (freedom).
Scott Joplin was awarded a posthumous Pulitzer Prize in 1976.
Joplin's 'The Entertainer' became popular again through the film The Sting (1973).
Charles Ives ran a successful insurance agency while composing.
Ives's Third Symphony won the 1947 Pulitzer Prize.
Claudio Monteverdi's L'Orfeo (1607) is among the earliest operas still performed.
Henry Purcell's Dido and Aeneas is one of the earliest English operas.
Purcell is buried in Westminster Abbey beneath the organ.
Johann Pachelbel was a friend of Bach's family and taught Bach's older brother.
Pachelbel's Canon was little known until a 1968 recording made it famous.
Georg Philipp Telemann is one of the most prolific composers ever, with over 3,000 works.
Domenico Scarlatti wrote 555 keyboard sonatas.
Domenico Scarlatti spent much of his career in Spain at the royal court.
Christoph Willibald Gluck reformed opera to make drama more important than vocal display.
Niccolò Paganini was the most famous violin virtuoso of his time.
Paganini's Caprice No. 24 inspired variations by Brahms and Rachmaninoff.
Paganini's violin, 'Il Cannone', is kept in Genoa.
Offenbach's 'Infernal Galop' is the music for the can-can.
Charles Gounod's 'Ave Maria' adds a melody over Bach's first Prelude.
Gabriel Fauré's Requiem is gentle, leaving out the fearsome Dies irae.
Fauré became deaf late in life, like Beethoven.
Erik Satie's Gymnopédies were written in 1888.
Satie's 'Vexations' comes with a note suggesting it be played 840 times.
César Franck's only symphony is in D minor.
Bach's Air on the G String is an arrangement of a movement from his Orchestral Suite No. 3.
The famous 'Albinoni Adagio' was largely written by Remo Giazotto in the 20th century.
Hildegard of Bingen, a 12th-century abbess, is one of the earliest composers known by name.
The modern orchestra tunes to an A, usually played by the oboe.
Standard concert pitch today is A = 440 Hz.
The Leipzig Gewandhaus Orchestra traces its roots to 1743.
The New York Philharmonic, founded in 1842, is the oldest US orchestra.
The Vienna Philharmonic was founded in 1842.
The Berlin Philharmonic was founded in 1882.
The Boston Symphony Orchestra was founded in 1881.
The conductor's baton came into general use in the 19th century.
Jean-Baptiste Lully died after striking his foot with his conducting staff.
The piano was invented by Bartolomeo Cristofori in Italy around 1700.
'Piano' is short for 'pianoforte', meaning soft-loud.
A standard modern piano has 88 keys.
Antonio Stradivari made violins in Cremona; about 650 of his instruments survive.
The saxophone was invented by Adolphe Sax in the 1840s.
The clarinet was developed around 1700 by Johann Christoph Denner.
A modern harp has 47 strings and 7 pedals.
The celesta was patented by Auguste Mustel in Paris in 1886.
The theremin, invented around 1920, is played without being touched.
Carnegie Hall opened in 1891 with Tchaikovsky as guest conductor.
La Scala in Milan opened in 1778.
The Sydney Opera House opened in 1973.
The Metropolitan Opera opened in 1883 with Gounod's Faust.
The Met moved to Lincoln Center in 1966.
Vienna's Musikverein is famous for its 'Golden Hall'.
The Paris Opéra's Palais Garnier opened in 1875.
The Royal Albert Hall in London opened in 1871.
The BBC Proms began in 1895 at Queen's Hall in London.
Enrico Caruso was one of the first singers to become a recording star.
Marian Anderson sang at the Lincoln Memorial on Easter Sunday 1939 to 75,000 people.
Marian Anderson was the first Black singer to perform at the Met, in 1955.
Van Cliburn won the first International Tchaikovsky Competition in Moscow in 1958.
Van Cliburn received a ticker-tape parade in New York after his 1958 win.
Vladimir Horowitz returned to the USSR to perform in 1986 after 61 years away.
Arturo Toscanini conducted from memory because of poor eyesight.
Toscanini led the NBC Symphony Orchestra, created for him in 1937.
Jascha Heifetz made his Carnegie Hall debut in 1917 at age 16.
Pablo Casals revived Bach's Cello Suites after finding the music in a shop as a teenager.
Casals played for President Kennedy at the White House in 1961.
Yo-Yo Ma performed for President Kennedy as a child in 1962.
Itzhak Perlman contracted polio at age 4 and performs seated.
Luciano Pavarotti, Plácido Domingo and José Carreras first sang as the Three Tenors in 1990.
Maria Callas was born in New York City to Greek parents.
Jacqueline du Pré's recording of Elgar's Cello Concerto is legendary.
Glenn Gould's 1955 Goldberg Variations recording made him famous.
Glenn Gould retired from live concerts at 31 to focus on recording.
Arthur Rubinstein gave concerts into his late 80s.
Leopold Stokowski conducted and appeared in Disney's Fantasia.
Nadia Boulanger taught Copland, Glass, Piazzolla and Quincy Jones.
Nadia Boulanger was the first woman to conduct the New York Philharmonic, in 1939.
Andrés Segovia brought the classical guitar to the concert hall.
Clara Schumann was among the first pianists to perform from memory.
'Sonata' comes from Italian for 'sounded', meaning played rather than sung.
'Cantata' comes from Italian for 'sung'.
A 'symphony' usually has four movements.
'Opus' is Latin for 'work'; opus numbers order a composer's publications.
'Allegro' means fast and cheerful; 'adagio' means slow and at ease.
A 'cadenza' is a showy solo passage, often near the end of a concerto movement.
'Pizzicato' means plucking a string instead of bowing.
'A cappella' means singing without instruments.
A 'nocturne' is a dreamy piece evoking night; John Field invented the piano form.
'Bel canto' means 'beautiful singing' and describes early 19th-century Italian opera.
An 'overture' is the instrumental opening of an opera.
A 'libretto' is the text of an opera, Italian for 'little book'.
A 'fugue' weaves several voices imitating one main theme.
A 'requiem' is a Mass for the dead.
'Prima donna' means 'first lady', the leading soprano in an opera.
'Encore' is French for 'again'.
'Bravo' is for a man, 'brava' for a woman, and 'bravi' for a group.
A 'leitmotif' is a recurring theme for a character or idea.
'Tempo' is Italian for 'time' and means the speed of music.
'Crescendo' means gradually getting louder.
The earliest known complete surviving song with notation is the Seikilos epitaph, about 2,000 years old.
Guido of Arezzo developed early music notation around 1000 AD.
'Do-re-mi' syllables come from a medieval hymn to St John the Baptist.
Thomas Edison recorded 'Mary Had a Little Lamb' on his phonograph in 1877.
The Pulitzer Prize for Music was first awarded in 1943, to William Schuman.
John Cage's 4′33″ is performed with no notes played.
Hymn tune 'Amazing Grace' words were written by John Newton, a former slave trader.
'Silent Night' was first performed on Christmas Eve 1818 in Oberndorf, Austria.
'Silent Night' was first accompanied on guitar.
Handel's Messiah is traditionally sung at Christmas, though it premiered at Easter time.
The Tchaikovsky Competition is held about every four years in Moscow.
The Chopin Competition in Warsaw is held every five years.
Disney's Fantasia (1940) featured music by Bach, Tchaikovsky, Stravinsky and others.
The Looney Tunes cartoon 'What's Opera, Doc?' parodies Wagner.
Bugs Bunny's 'The Rabbit of Seville' parodies Rossini's Barber of Seville.
Mozart's 'Twinkle' variations are on a French tune, 'Ah vous dirai-je, maman'.
'Twinkle, Twinkle', the ABC song and 'Baa Baa Black Sheep' share the same melody.
Brahms, Bach and Beethoven are called 'the Three Bs'.
Haydn's head was stolen after his burial and only reunited with his body in 1954.
Mozart and Haydn were close friends and played string quartets together.
Bach and Handel were born a month apart, about 80 miles apart, but never met.
Liszt and Chopin were friends in Paris in the 1830s.
Mahler, Bruckner and Brahms all lived in Vienna at the same time.
Stravinsky and Rachmaninoff both lived in Los Angeles in the 1940s.
Schoenberg and Gershwin played tennis together in Los Angeles.
Johann Strauss II and Brahms were friends; Brahms admired the Blue Danube.
Mendelssohn's Wedding March was played at the 1858 wedding of Victoria, Princess Royal.
Fanny Mendelssohn published some of her songs under her brother Felix's name.
Florence Price was the first African-American woman to have a symphony played by a major US orchestra, in 1933.
Amy Beach was the first American woman to have a symphony published, the 'Gaelic' (1896).
Lili Boulanger was the first woman to win the Prix de Rome, in 1913.
Ethel Smyth's 'The March of the Women' became an anthem for the suffragettes.
Barbara Strozzi published more secular music than any composer of her time in Venice.
Cécile Chaminade was the first female composer awarded France's Legion of Honour.
Marin Alsop became the first woman to conduct the Last Night of the Proms, in 2013.
Jennifer Higdon won the 2010 Pulitzer Prize for her Violin Concerto.
Ellen Taaffe Zwilich was the first woman to win the Pulitzer Prize for Music, in 1983.
Philip Glass's opera Einstein on the Beach (1976) lasts about five hours.
John Williams has received over 50 Oscar nominations.
Arvo Pärt's 'tintinnabuli' style imitates the ringing of bells.
Steve Reich's Music for 18 Musicians is a landmark of minimalism.
John Adams's Nixon in China premiered at Houston Grand Opera in 1987.
Olivier Messiaen wrote Quartet for the End of Time in a prisoner-of-war camp.
Messiaen transcribed hundreds of bird songs into music.
Arnold Schoenberg developed the twelve-tone method.
Schoenberg had a strong fear of the number 13.
Béla Bartók collected thousands of folk songs from Hungary and beyond.
Bartók's Concerto for Orchestra was commissioned by Serge Koussevitzky in 1943.
Benjamin Britten founded the Aldeburgh Festival in 1948.
Britten's War Requiem was written for the consecration of the new Coventry Cathedral in 1962.
Carl Orff's 'O Fortuna' opens and closes Carmina Burana.
Heitor Villa-Lobos wrote nine Bachianas Brasileiras blending Bach with Brazilian music.
Astor Piazzolla brought tango to the concert hall.
Erich Korngold was a child prodigy who later won Oscars for Hollywood scores.
Sergei Prokofiev's music for Alexander Nevsky was a landmark film score.
Bernard Herrmann wrote the shrieking strings for Hitchcock's Psycho.
Mendelssohn's sister Fanny was also a gifted composer, writing over 450 works.
